# Stress-Test Report: deadreckon Team-Sync Design

## Claim 1: `octocrab` is the right Rust GitHub client

**Verdict: Confirmed (with caveats)**

**Evidence:**
- Active and current. Latest release is **v0.50.0 (May 5, 2026)** with releases roughly monthly across v0.49.x in March/April 2026. Stars ~1.4k, 341 forks. ([octocrab on GitHub](https://github.com/XAMPPRocky/octocrab), [releases](https://github.com/XAMPPRocky/octocrab/releases))
- Coverage: dedicated handlers for `checks`, `pulls` (incl. drafts), `commits`, releases, and GraphQL. ([octocrab docs](https://docs.rs/octocrab)).
- Auth: PAT (`personal_token`), GitHub App via `OctocrabBuilder::app` with `create_jwt` and per-installation token acquisition (cached and auto-refreshed), plus OAuth token exchange added in v0.50. ([`octocrab::auth`](https://docs.rs/octocrab/latest/octocrab/auth/index.html))
- Tokio-native (async-trait, hyper). ETag support exists via typed `Etagged<T>` and `.etag()` builder methods (efficient polling).
- Rate-limit handling is **partial**: there's a `ratelimit` handler module and v0.49.7 added "rate limit handling for retries", but the README explicitly warns about pagination: *"There's no rate limiting so be careful."* You must implement client-side throttling for bulk write loops.
- Configurable `base_uri` for GitHub Enterprise.
- Breaking changes are infrequent — a notable one in v0.50.0 (removed `either` dep), otherwise additive across v0.49.x.

**Alternatives:** `hubcaps` is dead (last release ~2021); `github-rs` likewise stale; `gh` Go SDK is not Rust. Hand-rolled `reqwest` is viable for a small surface (we likely touch only ~10 endpoints) but loses GitHub App JWT logic, retry hooks, and ETag types. Octocrab is the right choice.

**Implication:** Use octocrab. Implement our own simple budget for write-loop endpoints (PR body, notes-related calls). Don't lean on the built-in retry handler for primary loop pacing.

---

## Claim 2: `gh auth token` inheritance is a viable auth path

**Verdict: Confirmed**

**Evidence:**
- `gh auth token` prints the token to stdout and is documented as non-interactive — no TTY required. ([gh auth token](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_auth_token))
- Multi-account: since gh v2.40, `gh` supports multiple accounts per host. By default `gh auth token` returns the *active* account's token; `--user <login>` and `--hostname <host>` disambiguate. ([cli/cli multiple-accounts.md](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cli/cli/trunk/docs/multiple-accounts.md))
- Cross-platform: works on macOS, Linux, Windows. The credential **storage** behind it varies (Keychain / libsecret / Windows Credential Manager / encrypted file fallback), but `gh auth token` abstracts that.
- Default scopes from `gh auth login --web`: `repo`, `read:org`, `gist`, `workflow`. Sufficient for branch push, PR create/update, commit comments, statuses. **Not** sufficient for Check Runs — see Claim 4.
- Failure modes: SSO-not-authorized returns a token that 401/403s on org repos; expired tokens are detectable via `/user` ping; fine-grained PATs honor only declared permissions.

**Implication:** Viable. The CLI should call `gh auth token` lazily, cache for the session, and on 401/403 print "your `gh` token may need `gh auth refresh` or SSO re-authorization."

---

## Claim 3: `keyring` (open-source-cooperative/keyring-rs) is the right Rust keyring

**Verdict: Partially confirmed**

**Evidence:**
- The crate moved from hwchen to **open-source-cooperative**, now maintained by Dan Brotsky. The original `keyring` crate is now a thin "sample code" facade; the real work is in `keyring-core` plus per-platform store crates. ([keyring-rs](https://github.com/open-source-cooperative/keyring-rs), [crates.io](https://crates.io/crates/keyring))
- Linux is the painful platform: depends on `secret-service` (zbus pure-Rust async) or `dbus-secret-service` (libdbus C binding). Either way it requires a running Secret Service daemon (gnome-keyring, KWallet). On headless Linux/CI, this fails — the maintainers explicitly link to a workaround that starts a Gnome keyring unlocked with a known password. ([keyring docs Linux note](https://docs.rs/keyring/latest/keyring/secret_service/index.html))
- Dependency weight on Linux (zbus 4 + crypto features) is non-trivial but acceptable.
- No conflict with `gh`'s own keychain entries — different service names; they coexist, though it means a user could have two stored tokens (one per tool).

**Alternatives:** `secret-service` directly (Linux-only, more code), or simply *don't* persist a token of our own and always defer to `gh auth token`. The latter is the cleanest fallback for headless boxes.

**Implication:** Make `keyring` **optional**, behind a feature flag. On headless Linux, gracefully degrade to "env var > `gh auth token`" with no keyring write attempt. Don't fail to start because dbus is absent.

---

## Claim 4: GitHub Check Runs work for our use case

**Verdict: BROKEN for the primary OSS path**

**Evidence (this is the killer finding):**
- GitHub's REST docs are explicit: *"OAuth apps and personal access tokens (classic) cannot use this endpoint"* on update. Create likewise restricts write access to GitHub Apps. ([REST API for check runs](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/checks/runs))
- Fine-grained PATs cannot even *select* a Checks permission in the UI. GitHub support has confirmed: *"It isn't possible to assign Checks permissions to a Fine-grained PAT — only GitHub Apps can access this API."* ([community discussion #129512](https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/129512))
- One community comment claims classic PATs work for the Checks API, but GitHub's own REST docs contradict this for the write endpoints. Even if it works today via `repo` scope, it's an undocumented edge that GitHub is actively deprecating.
- UI: GitHub App–owned check runs render with the App's avatar in the Checks tab. PAT-owned ones (where they work at all) appear as user activity, not first-class checks.

**Alternative — Commit Statuses API:** [`POST /repos/{owner}/{repo}/statuses/{sha}`](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/commits/statuses) accepts a classic PAT with `repo:status` (or `repo`), and a fine-grained PAT with the **Commit statuses: write** permission. Renders as the older grey/yellow/green dot in the PR UI, with a `context`, `description`, and `target_url`. Less rich (no markdown body, no annotations) but PAT-friendly and works today.

**Implication — the design must change:**
- Drop Check Runs from the v1 OSS path. Use **Commit Statuses** with a stable `context` like `deadreckon/<run-id>` and a description like "turn 14/30 — running". Link `target_url` to the `.deadreckon/runs/<id>/INDEX.md` blob URL.
- Reserve Check Runs as an *optional* enhancement when the user installs an actual deadreckon GitHub App on their org (treat as the "premium" surfacing path, not the default).

---

## Claim 5: Git notes (`refs/notes/dr-runs`) are a viable team index

**Verdict: Broken**

**Evidence:**
- GitHub stopped rendering notes in its UI in 2014 and has not reinstated. Notes are invisible to anyone using the web UI. ([Git Notes: git's coolest, most unloved feature](https://tylercipriani.com/blog/2022/11/19/git-notes-gits-coolest-most-unloved-feature/))
- Adoption is genuinely thin. Most Git GUIs (GitHub Desktop, GitKraken, VS Code Git panel) don't surface notes. The intuition is correct.
- `refs/notes/*` is **not in the default fetch refspec** — every teammate must manually configure `fetch = +refs/notes/*:refs/notes/*` or invoke `git fetch origin "refs/notes/*:refs/notes/*"` explicitly. ([git-notes docs](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-notes))
- Concurrent writes: documented race in semantic-release CI shows `! [rejected] refs/notes/... (fetch first)` when two processes push notes to the same ref. `git notes merge` works *but* defaults to **manual** strategy (drops a `.git/NOTES_MERGE_WORKTREE` and waits for human intervention). Auto strategies (`union`, `cat_sort_uniq`, `theirs`, `ours`) exist but must be configured explicitly. ([git-notes merge strategies](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-notes))
- Even `union` only concatenates — for structured per-commit JSON, you'd need a custom merge driver.

**Alternative — `.deadreckon/team-index.jsonl`:** A normal tracked file, append-only JSONL, one line per turn or run-state change. Rebase/merge with a simple union driver (or just sort+uniq via .gitattributes). Pros: visible in PR diffs, searchable in GitHub UI, no extra fetch ritual, works on every host. Cons: shows up in PR diffs (noisy unless gitignored on dev branches).

**Implication — the design must change:**
- Drop `refs/notes/dr-runs` as the team index. Use a committed `.deadreckon/index/<run-id>.json` (or single `.deadreckon/team-index.jsonl`) with a documented `union` merge driver. Notes can remain a "power user" optional sync, but not the primary cross-team surface.

---

## Claim 6: GitHub API rate limits are manageable for per-turn PR body updates

**Verdict: Partially confirmed — secondary limits are the real risk**

**Evidence:**
- Primary: 5,000 req/hr authenticated user; 15,000/hr for GitHub Apps on Enterprise. ([rate limits](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/using-the-rest-api/rate-limits-for-the-rest-api))
- **Secondary content-creation limits**: *"no more than 80 content-generating requests per minute and no more than 500 content-generating requests per hour"*. PR body updates are content-generating. ([rate limits](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/using-the-rest-api/rate-limits-for-the-rest-api))
- A 200-turn run that updates the PR body once per turn is comfortably under 500/hr **only if** turns are slower than ~7 seconds on average. Bursts of fast turns will trigger 429 with a `Retry-After`.
- Octocrab supports ETags via `Etagged<T>`, useful for read polling but not for write deduplication.
- Renovate and Dependabot batch comment/PR updates rather than streaming. They explicitly debounce.

**Implication:**
- Don't update the PR body per turn. Coalesce: write turn-level state to `.deadreckon/runs/<id>/turn-N.json` (cheap git operation), and only PATCH the PR body on (a) phase change, (b) every Nth turn, or (c) a 30-second debounce — whichever comes first. Honor `Retry-After` on 429.
- For the "live" surface, prefer commit statuses (also content-generating, but smaller payloads and arguably more idiomatic for "current state").

---

## Claim 7: Draft PRs can be created on push without prior PR existence

**Verdict: Partially confirmed**

**Evidence:**
- `gh pr create --draft` (and `POST /repos/{o}/{r}/pulls` with `draft: true`) requires **at least one commit** between the head and base. Empty branches produce `No commits between main and <branch>`. ([cli/cli #9112](https://github.com/cli/cli/issues/9112), [#2691](https://github.com/cli/cli/issues/2691))
- One commit is sufficient. The PR can be created the moment the first commit is pushed.
- The PAT user must have either push access to the upstream or be pushing to a fork; cross-repo PRs work, but the head must reference `fork-owner:branch`.
- Base branch auto-detection: gh uses the repo's default branch unless `--base` is given.

**Implication:**
- The design's "push branch then open draft PR" works as long as the first turn produces at least an empty commit (`git commit --allow-empty -m "deadreckon: run started"` is the safe primitive). Document this explicitly in the run-start sequence.

---

## Claim 8: GitHub repo permissions are sufficient ACL

**Verdict: Partially confirmed**

**Evidence:**
- A `repo`-scoped PAT inherits the user's full permissions, including any branch-protection bypass roles assigned to that user.
- Branch protection by default protects only the explicit branches/patterns configured (typically `main`, `release/*`). The `dr/*` namespace is exempt unless the org admin explicitly added it. Wildcard rules use `fnmatch` and don't cross `/`. ([branch protection rules](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-protected-branches/managing-a-branch-protection-rule))
- Force-push to `dr/*` works by default. A locked-down org might add a `*` or `**/*` wildcard — handle the failure gracefully.
- Forks: if the contributor has no push to upstream, the standard fork-and-PR flow works, but our CLI must detect "no push access" and offer to push to `origin` (assumed to be the user's fork) and open the PR `head: <user>:dr/<id>`. ([about forks](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/collaborating-with-pull-requests/working-with-forks/about-permissions-and-visibility-of-forks))

**Implication:**
- Probe push access at startup (cheap `gh api repos/o/r --jq .permissions.push`). On failure, switch to fork mode automatically: ensure a fork exists (`gh repo fork --remote`), push to the fork, open PR upstream.
- Document that `dr/*` should not be added to branch-protection wildcards.

---

## Claim 9: `keyring` + `gh auth token` + env-var three-tier auth is the right pattern

**Verdict: Partially confirmed — order should change**

**Evidence:**
- Common patterns in Rust GitHub-adjacent CLIs (cargo-binstall, cargo-dist) generally use: env var (`GITHUB_TOKEN`/`GH_TOKEN`) first, then `gh` if available, with no native keyring.
- In Codespaces, `GITHUB_TOKEN` is auto-injected with restricted scope. There's a known issue where gh prefers `GITHUB_TOKEN` over its own stored token in Codespaces. ([cli/cli #6238](https://github.com/cli/cli/issues/6238))
- Order: gh's own precedence is `GH_TOKEN > GITHUB_TOKEN > stored credentials`. Mirroring this is least surprising.

**Implication — the design should change:**
- Order: `GH_TOKEN` > `GITHUB_TOKEN` > keyring > `gh auth token` > prompt. (gh-token last because gh itself may have been logged out, and keyring lets us persist a token across machines that don't have gh.)
- In Codespaces, the auto-injected `GITHUB_TOKEN` is restricted to the current repo and may lack PR write — detect Codespaces (`CODESPACES=true`) and warn if scopes are insufficient.
- Make keyring optional (Claim 3).

---

## Claim 10: Solo users see zero behavior change

**Verdict: Confirmed**

**Evidence:**
- `git remote -v` reliably exposes the URL; parsing for `github.com` (or `*.ghe.com` / configured Enterprise host) is straightforward via regex on both SSH (`git@github.com:o/r.git`) and HTTPS (`https://github.com/o/r(.git)?`).
- octocrab's `base_uri` makes self-hosted GHES first-class.
- Detection cascade: no remote → skip. Remote not GitHub → skip. GitHub remote, no token available → log a one-line "team-sync disabled (no auth)" and continue solo.

**Implication:**
- Hard-gate every team-sync code path on `is_github_repo() && has_token()`. Never call into octocrab at startup unconditionally. Solo mode must produce zero network traffic.

---

# The design must change in these 7 ways

1. **Replace Check Runs with Commit Statuses** as the v1 PR-UI surface (Claim 4). Reserve Check Runs as a future GitHub App tier.
2. **Replace `refs/notes/dr-runs` with a committed JSONL/JSON team index** under `.deadreckon/` (Claim 5). Drop notes from the v1 design entirely or reframe as opt-in extra.
3. **Debounce/coalesce PR body updates** to stay under the 500/hr secondary content-creation limit; honor `Retry-After` (Claim 6).
4. **Make `keyring` optional and feature-gated**, with graceful fallback on headless Linux/CI where Secret Service is absent (Claim 3).
5. **Seed runs with an empty commit** before opening the draft PR, since GitHub rejects PRs with zero commits between head and base (Claim 7).
6. **Reorder auth precedence to `GH_TOKEN > GITHUB_TOKEN > keyring > gh auth token > prompt`** and special-case Codespaces' restricted token (Claim 9).
7. **Detect push access and switch to fork-mode automatically** for contributors without upstream write; document that `dr/*` must not be branch-protected (Claim 8).

Stress-test every load-bearing technical claim in a proposed deadreckon team-sync design. The design proposes that a Rust CLI use GitHub primitives — pushed branches, draft PRs, GitHub Check Runs, git notes (`refs/notes/dr-runs`), and committed `.deadreckon/runs/<id>/` artifacts — to make agentic-CLI runs visible and resumable across a team. Auth via `gh auth token` inheritance + OS keyring + env var. Wired with `octocrab` (GitHub client) and `keyring` (token storage).

Many claims I made about this design are intuition, not verified. Your job is to confirm or break each one.

## Claims to validate

### Claim 1: `octocrab` is the right Rust GitHub client

- Maturity: stars, last release, active maintainers, breaking-change cadence.
- Coverage: does it actually support draft PRs, Check Runs (create + update), commit comments, releases?
- Async story: tokio-compat? rate-limit handling built in or DIY?
- Auth: PAT, GitHub App JWT, OAuth — which does it support? How clean?
- Alternatives worth knowing: `hubcaps` (dead?), `github-rs` (?), GraphQL clients, or rolling-our-own with `reqwest`. Compare honestly.

### Claim 2: `gh auth token` inheritance is a viable auth path

- Verify the actual command and behavior of `gh auth token` (does it print the token to stdout? does it require a TTY? does it work in CI?).
- What happens when the user has multiple GitHub accounts in `gh`? (`gh auth status` shows them; `gh auth token` returns which?)
- Cross-platform behavior: macOS, Linux, Windows, WSL — any differences?
- Token scopes that `gh auth login --web` grants by default — are they sufficient for our needs (we'd need `repo`, `pull_request`, possibly `checks:write`)?
- Failure modes: token expired, SSO not authorized, fine-grained PATs vs classic PATs.

### Claim 3: `keyring` (Hwchen's crate) is the right Rust keyring

- Maturity, platform support, transitive dep weight (esp. on Linux where Secret Service is required).
- Headless Linux behavior — does it gracefully degrade when there's no Secret Service (CI, minimal containers)?
- Conflicts with `gh`'s own keychain entries.
- Alternatives: `secret-service` (Linux-only), rolling-our-own.

### Claim 4: GitHub Check Runs work for our use case

This is critical. Verify:
- **Auth requirement**: do Check Runs require a registered GitHub App (with installation), or can a regular PAT post Check Runs? This is the killer question — if Check Runs require a GitHub App, the elegant story collapses for OSS users who don't want to install a deadreckon app on their org.
- If a PAT works, what scopes? `repo` only, or `checks:write`? Are the latter even available on classic PATs?
- Check Run lifecycle: queued → in_progress → completed; can a PAT-owned check be updated by the same PAT later? Cross-machine?
- UI surfacing: does a Check Run from a PAT look as official in the PR UI as one from a GitHub App? (Screenshots / docs.)
- Alternative: **commit statuses** (the older API). Less rich UI but PAT-friendly. Compare.

### Claim 5: Git notes (`refs/notes/dr-runs`) are a viable team index

- **Adoption reality check**: how widely are git notes actually used in 2026? My intuition says "almost nobody uses them" — verify or break this. Search for criticism, dropped support, GitHub UI rendering of notes.
- Does GitHub render notes in the PR/commit UI? (Last I checked, no — they exist via API and `git fetch` only.)
- Sync mechanics: is `git fetch refs/notes/*` reliable? Does it conflict on concurrent writes (two teammates writing notes to the same ref simultaneously)?
- Conflict resolution: notes use a tree-of-blobs model — what happens when Alice and Bob both add a note to the same commit? Does `git notes merge` actually work?
- Alternative: a single `.deadreckon/team-index.jsonl` file in the repo, append-only. Compare honestly.

### Claim 6: GitHub API rate limits are manageable for per-turn PR body updates

- Authenticated user rate limit: 5000/hr. GitHub App rate limit: higher. Secondary rate limits (concurrent requests, content creation throttle).
- A long deadreckon run might do 50–200 turns. If we update the PR body once per turn, that's 200 API calls. Is that fine, or does it bump into secondary rate limits?
- Best practices for batching PR body updates? Do other tools (Renovate, Dependabot) have published patterns?
- Conditional requests (ETag / If-None-Match) — does octocrab support them?

### Claim 7: Draft PRs can be created on push without prior PR existence

- Confirm: can `gh pr create --draft` (or octocrab equivalent) create a draft PR immediately when the branch has only one commit? What about zero commits (just an empty branch)?
- Permissions needed (the PAT user must have write access to the repo, or be on a fork — what about contributors who only have a fork)?
- Auto-detection of base branch — what's the convention?

### Claim 8: GitHub repo permissions are sufficient ACL

- Verify: a PAT with `repo` scope inherits the user's full repo permissions, including branch protection bypass settings.
- Branch protection: does it block force-push to `dr/...` branches? Most repos protect only main; verify our `dr/` namespace is exempt by default.
- Fork workflows: if a contributor doesn't have push access to the upstream, the design has to handle "push to my fork, open PR against upstream." Does our flow degrade gracefully?

### Claim 9: `keyring` + `gh auth token` + env-var three-tier auth is the right pattern

- Are there published patterns for this in popular Rust CLIs that integrate with GitHub? `cargo-binstall`, `cargo-dist`, `dprint`, `cargo-mutants`, etc. — what do they do?
- The order I proposed (env > keyring > `gh`): correct, or should it be `gh` first?
- What about Codespaces, where `GITHUB_TOKEN` is auto-injected? Should we prefer that?

### Claim 10: Solo users see zero behavior change

- Does `git remote -v` reliably indicate "this is a GitHub repo"? (parse `github.com` host)
- For self-hosted GitHub Enterprise, does the same flow work? `octocrab` configurable base URL?
- For users with no GitHub remote (private gitlab, no remote at all), the flow must short-circuit silently — confirm there's no path that requires GitHub auth even for solo runs.

## Deliverable

A focused written report (~1500–2200 words). For EACH of the 10 claims:

- **Verdict**: Confirmed / Broken / Partially confirmed / Unverifiable
- **Evidence**: cite docs, GitHub source, octocrab source, blog posts, etc. with `[label](url)`
- **Implication for the design**: if broken/partial, what does the design have to change?

End with a **"the design must change in these N ways"** summary section that surfaces the must-fix list.

WebSearch and WebFetch liberally. Read crate `Cargo.toml`s, read GitHub API reference docs, read `gh` CLI source if needed.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about stacked PRs adoption and the tools you asked about:

## Stacked PRs and Tool Adoption

Modern tools like Graphite, ghstack, spr, and Sapling automate stacked PR workflows, making this development approach more practical. Teams that adopt stacking often break work into 5–10 smaller PRs instead of one massive one, with benefits including faster reviews and higher-quality code.

## Graphite vs. Sapling

**Sapling** and **Graphite** represent different approaches to stacked PRs:

- Sapling is a source control system with a CLI and review interface that sits on top of GitHub, inspired by Mercurial and Phabricator used internally at Meta, and is maintained by Meta Open Source.

- While Sapling is a full-fledged source control system originally designed at Meta to address massive monorepo challenges, Graphite builds on top of Git itself, offering a lightweight but powerful workflow layer.

## Recent 2025-2026 Developments

Graphite retains advantages in squash merge compatibility, conflict resolution UX, and stack visualization maturity, though integrated features that are "good enough" tend to displace specialized external tools over time.

Additionally, recent developments include GitHub's native stacked PR support and Sapling's approach of stacking at the commit level rather than the branch level.

## What is Pre-Commit?

The pre-commit framework is a framework for managing and maintaining multi-language pre-commit hooks. Git hook scripts are useful for identifying simple issues before submission to code review, and the framework runs hooks on every commit to automatically point out issues in code such as missing semicolons, trailing whitespace, and debug statements.

## Why Universal Git Hooks?

As projects grow, sharing pre-commit hooks across projects is painful because developers copy and paste unwieldy bash scripts from project to project and have to manually change the hooks to work for different project structures. While you can write hooks as simple shell scripts in .git/hooks/, managing them becomes complex as your project grows, which is where the pre-commit framework shines—it provides a standardized way to manage and share hooks across your team.

## Key Adoption Benefits in 2025

Pre-commit hooks provide instant feedback right when you commit, while CI/CD pipelines might take minutes to run. The key to successful adoption lies in balancing thoroughness with developer experience, as fast, focused hooks that provide immediate value will become an indispensable part of your team's workflow.

One nearly undisputed benefit of pre-commit hooks is preventing secrets from being committed—tools like Gitleaks can scan for accidentally committed API keys or passwords, and catching this locally is a massive security win, so many teams find the setup cost of hooks justified.

## 2025 Trends

The search results reveal an emerging competitor: prek is a complete re-implementation of the pre-commit framework built in Rust instead of Python designed to be a drop-in replacement, and it's already been adopted by CPython, Apache Airflow, FastAPI, Ruff, and dozens more.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about GitHub organization PAT restrictions with SSO and enterprise SAML scope blocking:

## PAT Authorization Requirements with SAML SSO

When SAML SSO is required, you must authorize your SSH key or Personal Access Token (PAT) to access organization resources. When a GitHub organization enforces SAML SSO, all PATs must be explicitly authorized for use by the organization. If this step is skipped or the organization has changed its SSO enforcement, Git operations like git-upload-pack will be denied — even if the PAT has the correct scopes.

## Token Scope Blocking

You must authorize your personal access token (classic) after creation before the token can access an organization that uses SAML single sign-on (SSO). Additionally, the scopes in a personal access token are edited, or the token is regenerated. can revoke authorization.

## Fine-Grained PATs vs. Classic PATs

Fine-grained personal access tokens are authorized during token creation, before access to the organization is granted. This differs from classic PATs, which require post-creation authorization.

## Enterprise-Level SAML Configuration

To access each organization's protected resources using the API and Git, the member must use a personal access token or SSH key that the member has authorized for use with the organization. Members will need to authorize any PATs, SSH keys, OAuth apps, and GitHub Apps that were never authorized for use with SAML SSO for the organization.

The key takeaway is that PAT authorization is a separate step from token creation when SAML SSO is enforced, and scope restrictions alone won't allow access without proper authorization.

## Basic Behavior

The `gh auth token` command outputs the authentication token for an account on a given GitHub host. Without the --hostname flag, the default host is chosen.

## Multiple Account Support

The `gh auth token` command has been extended with a `--user` flag, which in combination with `--hostname` can be used to disambiguate accounts when running non-interactively.

## Token Behavior with Account Switching

Switching the "active" user for a host will swap the token used by gh for API requests, and for git operations when gh was configured as a git credential manager.

## Recent Updates

According to a recent issue from November 2025, gh auth switch will also update which account git uses. This indicates that the behavior has been refined in the latest version to make token and credential management more consistent across different `gh auth` commands.

The key takeaway is that when you have multiple accounts configured, you can use the `--user` flag with `gh auth token` to retrieve tokens for specific accounts non-interactively, while the active account determines which token is used by default.

Based on the search results, here's a comprehensive comparison of GitHub Check Runs API access using Personal Access Tokens (PAT) versus GitHub Apps:

## Key Difference: Check Runs API Availability

The REST API to manage check runs and check suites is only available to GitHub Apps. This is a critical limitation for PATs.

Specifically, at the moment, it isn't possible to assign Checks permissions to a Fine-grained PAT—only GitHub Apps can access this API. However, classic tokens also work for the Checks API, though fine-grained PATs do not.

## General PAT vs GitHub App Comparison

**Personal Access Tokens (PATs):**
- Personal access tokens are intended to access GitHub resources on behalf of yourself.
- PATs are associated with a specific-user, so if these tokens are associated with a workflow, the original user who created the token must manage the lifecycle of these tokens.
- If your token gets leaked, someone could have full access to your resources.

**GitHub Apps:**
- For long-lived integrations, you should use a GitHub App.
- GitHub Applications allow for short-lived credentials which are associated with an organization to be created, instead of an individual. By default, the tokens generated by GitHub Apps have an expiration time of 8 hours.
- GitHub Apps have their own permissions, independent of any user. Permissions are more granular.

## Recommendation

If you need to use the Check Runs API, you must use a GitHub App rather than a fine-grained PAT. Classic PATs may work as an alternative, but GitHub Apps are the recommended and more secure approach.

The act tool allows developers to run GitHub Actions locally, providing a more convenient way to test and iterate on workflows before pushing them to GitHub.

## Local Adoption Benefits

Act reads your workflow files under .github/workflows/ and uses Docker to simulate the GitHub Actions environment, spinning up each job inside a Docker container as if it were running on GitHub, complete with the same environment variables and file system layout.

Secrets and environment variables can be passed effortlessly to workflows with act, perfectly emulating the GitHub environment.

## PR Convention & Adoption

To check that PRs contain a changeset, we recommend using the changeset bot, or if you want to fail builds on a changesets failure, run yarn changeset status in CI. Each pull request can include a changeset file that explicitly states how the package version should be updated and why.

While this can be used to add a CI check for changesets, we recommend not doing this. We instead recommend using the changeset bot to detect pull requests missing changesets, as not all pull requests need one.

## Recent 2025 Adoption

Recent guides from 2025 show strong adoption of Changesets with monorepos. Moving to a monorepo setup with pnpm and changesets has been a game changer, and Changesets is recommended because it's intuitive to use, and - just like Turborepo - fits with the monorepo tools you're already used to.

## Automation & Workflow

To make releasing easier, you can use this changesets github action to automate creating versioning pull requests, and optionally publishing packages.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about git notes adoption and real-world usage:

## Adoption and Obscurity

Git notes are relegated to obscurity, hamstrung by an obscure and clunky interface and limited adoption. Although git notes has been part of Git for more than a decade, despite its potential, it has not gained widespread adoption or recognition among developers.

## Why Adoption is Limited

Several factors contribute to poor adoption:

- **Usability Issues**: One contributing factor to underutilization is its quirky nature and relatively complex usage, as the process of adding and managing notes is not as straightforward or intuitive as other Git commands.

- **Tool Support**: Not many GUI tools support git notes, and if your team's favorite git tool doesn't support the feature, it's difficult to convince teams to adopt it. GitHub used to support git notes but removed the feature some years ago.

- **Sharing Problems**: Another drawback is that git notes are not automatically shared.

- **Performance Concerns**: Notes for the entire repository are stored in a flat tree where each entry has the target object's name as filename, meaning every commit access has to perform a linear scan through the tree.

## Real-World Use Cases

Despite limited adoption, they're cool for appending notes from automated systems like ticket or build systems, and a common use is tacking metadata onto commits, allowing you to amend new information about old commits in a special namespace.

Based on the search results, here are the key findings about GitHub Check Runs API third-party integration adoption challenges:

## Permission and Authentication Barriers

One of the primary challenges is the restrictive permission model. Write permission for the REST API to interact with checks is only available to GitHub Apps. OAuth apps and authenticated users can view check runs and check suites, but they are not able to create them. This significantly limits which types of third-party applications can actually create check runs, forcing developers to build full GitHub Apps rather than simpler OAuth applications.

## Limited Scope for Third-Party Integrations

Write permission for the REST API to interact with checks is only available to GitHub Apps. OAuth apps and authenticated users can view check runs and check suites, but they are not able to create them. This architectural decision effectively restricts third-party integrations to read-only access, creating a barrier to adoption for services that want to provide CI/CD feedback or automation features.

## API Limitations

Additional technical challenges include the Checks API only looks for pushes in the repository where the check suite or check run were created. Pushes to a branch in a forked repository are not detected and return an empty pull_requests array. This limitation reduces the API's utility for certain workflows and integration patterns.

## Alternative Solutions

Rather than directly addressing these challenges, documentation suggests if you aren't building a GitHub App, you might be interested in using the REST API to interact with commit statuses as a workaround for those unable to use the Check Runs API.

The search results indicate that the main adoption challenge stems from GitHub's deliberate architectural decision to restrict check creation to first-party GitHub Apps only.

# Check Runs API Authorization Requirements

## Creating Check Runs

**GitHub App is required.** According to the documentation: "Write permission for the REST API to interact with checks is only available to GitHub Apps. OAuth apps and authenticated users can view check runs and check suites, but they are not able to create them."

Personal Access Tokens (classic or fine-grained) cannot create check runs.

## Updating Check Runs

**GitHub App is also required.** The update endpoint explicitly states: "OAuth apps and personal access tokens (classic) cannot use this endpoint."

## Reading Check Runs

Viewing check runs is accessible to OAuth apps and authenticated users with the `repo` scope on private repositories. However, this read-only access doesn't extend to creation or modification.

## Summary

- **Create/Update**: GitHub Apps only
- **Read**: OAuth apps and PATs with `repo` scope (for private repos)
- **Alternative**: If you can't use a GitHub App, consider using the commit statuses API instead

# gh auth token

## Purpose
This command outputs the authentication token for an account on a given GitHub host. It retrieves credentials rather than performing authentication itself.

## Output
Yes, it prints to stdout—the token is displayed as text output, suitable for capturing or piping to other commands.

## TTY Requirement
The documentation doesn't specify TTY requirements, so it appears to work in non-interactive contexts.

## Multi-Account Behavior
The command intelligently selects accounts:
- **Without `--hostname`**: Uses the default GitHub host
- **Without `--user`**: Uses the active account for that host
- **With both flags**: Retrieves the token for a specific user on a specific host

## Available Flags

| Flag | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `-h, --hostname <string>` | Specify the GitHub instance hostname |
| `-u, --user <string>` | Specify which account's token to retrieve |

This makes it flexible for scenarios involving multiple GitHub instances or accounts.

# Survey: precedents for the deadreckon team-sync pattern

## 1. Direct precedents — agent runs published as PRs

| Tool | Pattern | Adoption signal | What worked / didn't |
|---|---|---|---|
| **GitHub Copilot Workspace** (original) | Issue-to-PR via spec-plan-implement pipeline | Sunset May 30 2025; rebuilt as "Copilot coding agent" | The Workspace UI flopped; the *underlying issue→draft-PR→commits-as-turns* pattern was kept and rebranded ([GitHub Blog](https://github.blog/news-insights/product-news/github-copilot-meet-the-new-coding-agent/)) |
| **Copilot coding agent** | Assign issue to `@copilot`, agent pushes commits to a draft PR you can watch live | GA Sept 2025, available on Pro/Pro+/Business/Enterprise | Pricing complaints forced a "1 session = 1 premium request" rework — community wanted clearer cost per agent run ([GitHub Discussion #159068](https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/159068)) |
| **Devin (Cognition)** | Opens its own PRs against your repo | 67% PR merge rate (up from 34%); priced reset from $500 → $20/mo (96% cut) in Apr 2025 to drive adoption ([VentureBeat](https://venturebeat.com/programming-development/devin-2-0-is-here-cognition-slashes-price-of-ai-software-engineer-to-20-per-month-from-500)) | Users complained about unpredictable failures and Devin "spending days on impossible solutions" ([Cognition 2025 review](https://cognition.ai/blog/devin-annual-performance-review-2025), [The Register](https://www.theregister.com/2025/01/23/ai_developer_devin_poor_reviews/)) |
| **Cursor BugBot / background agents** | Bot opens PRs / pushes commits to a branch from an event | 35% of Autofix changes merged; 76% pre-merge bug resolution rate (up from 52%) ([Cursor blog](https://cursor.com/blog/bugbot-autofix)) | The "auto-fix on a PR you already opened" framing reduced noise vs. pure bot-PR firehose |
| **OpenAI Codex web** | Cloud agent in `chatgpt.com/codex` opens PRs in parallel | Available to ChatGPT Plus since June 2025; ranked #1 coding agent in Apr 2026 refreshes ([Codex docs](https://developers.openai.com/codex/cloud)) | Strong adoption when bundled with an existing subscription; weak as standalone |
| **Jules (Google)** | Issue → reviewable PR with critic review pre-submission | "Significantly less community buzz and adoption compared to Devin or Claude Code" as of Mar 2026; being rebuilt as "Jitro" ([Nelson's log](https://nelsonslog.wordpress.com/2026/03/18/first-impressions-of-jules-googles-coding-agent/), [TestingCatalog](https://www.testingcatalog.com/google-prepares-jules-v2-agent-capable-of-taking-bigger-tasks/)) | Pure issue-to-PR without strong context loop didn't differentiate |
| **Sweep.dev** | The original "GitHub issue → PR" tool of 2024 | **Pivoted away from GitHub-bot PRs to a JetBrains plugin** (40k+ installs, v1.27 in Dec 2025) ([sweep.dev](https://sweep.dev/), [docs.sweep.dev/changelog](https://docs.sweep.dev/changelog)) | Their original pattern (the one we're proposing) was abandoned by the company that pioneered it. Sweep.io (CRM) is a different company ([Sweep.io](https://www.sweep.io/blog/sweep-io-vs-sweep-ai-what-s-the-difference)) |
| **Sourcegraph Amp** | Threads-as-shareable-URLs, server-stored, leaderboards | Active development; "thread maps", labels, search-by-thread-ID added 2026 ([Amp news](https://ampcode.com/news), [Amp manual](https://ampcode.com/manual)) | The shareable-URL pattern is winning over commit-everything-to-git for transcripts |
| **Aider** | Local CLI; commits per turn, no PR integration | `aider` ships a `.gitignore` with `.aider*` to *prevent* committing chat history ([Aider FAQ](https://aider.chat/docs/faq.html)) | Deliberately rejected the "transcripts in git" pattern |

**Backlash signal — bot PR fatigue is documented.** Renovate's whole pitch over Dependabot is grouping PRs because "logging in on Monday morning to find 50 separate PRs leads to alert fatigue, where developers simply close PRs without looking" ([nesbitt.io best practices](https://nesbitt.io/2026/01/10/16-best-practices-for-reducing-dependabot-noise.html), [Renovate docs](https://docs.renovatebot.com/bot-comparison/)). Maintainer fatigue from agent-generated PRs is a named problem in 2026 — see the matplotlib incident where an agent published a "hit piece" after being rejected ([Fast Company](https://www.fastcompany.com/91492228/matplotlib-scott-shambaugh-opencla-ai-agent), [Socket.dev](https://socket.dev/blog/ai-agent-submits-pr-to-matplotlib-publishes-angry-blog-post-after-rejection)).

## 2. Run-artifact-in-git precedents

- **AGENTS.md** — adopted by 60,000+ repos; consolidated under the new Linux Foundation Agentic AI Foundation in Dec 2025 ([Linux Foundation press](https://www.linuxfoundation.org/press/linux-foundation-announces-the-formation-of-the-agentic-ai-foundation), [InfoQ](https://www.infoq.com/news/2025/08/agents-md/)). **Static config in git is a green light.**
- **`.cursor/rules/`** — committed widely; stable.
- **SpecStory `.specstory/history/`** — *transcripts* in git. Mixed reception: users have actively gitignored it because "everyone's files would be mixed in together"; the SpecStory team itself has a public discussion thread admitting the pattern needs work for teams ([SpecStory Discussion #48](https://github.com/specstoryai/getspecstory/discussions/48)). Spec-Kit has the same debate ([spec-kit #1437](https://github.com/github/spec-kit/discussions/1437), [#769](https://github.com/github/spec-kit/discussions/769)).
- **Aider chat history** — *deliberately gitignored* by default. Aider auto-writes `.aider*` into `.gitignore` ([Aider FAQ](https://aider.chat/docs/faq.html)). The most established agentic-CLI in the field rejected this pattern.
- **Continue.dev** — *config* in git is encouraged (`.continue/` dirs); transcripts/sessions go through Hub Configurations because committing them mixes API keys and creates churn ([Continue docs](https://docs.continue.dev/customize/deep-dives/configuration), [understanding-configs](https://docs.continue.dev/guides/understanding-configs)).
- **Sourcegraph Amp threads** — explicitly *not* in git; stored on Sourcegraph servers with shareable URLs ([Amp manual](https://ampcode.com/manual)).
- **OpenTelemetry GenAI traces** — invariably shipped to an observability backend, not committed.

**Pattern:** static config (AGENTS.md, .cursor/rules) wins in git; *per-turn transcripts* are either gitignored (Aider) or routed to a server (Amp, Continue Hub). SpecStory is the closest precedent for our pattern, and it's actively wrestling with the team-coordination cost.

## 3. Git notes reality check

The good news: notes work and are still in use. Gerrit's `refs/notes/review` continues to attach review metadata in production ([Gerrit reviewnotes](https://gerrit.googlesource.com/plugins/reviewnotes/+/refs/heads/master/src/main/resources/Documentation/refs-notes-review.md)). A 2025 tool, [git-ai](https://github.com/git-ai-project/git-ai), uses notes to track AI-attributed commits — direct precedent for our use case.

The bad news: **GitHub stopped rendering commit notes in 2014 and has not changed** ([Tyler Cipriani](https://tylercipriani.com/blog/2022/11/19/git-notes-gits-coolest-most-unloved-feature/)). Google's `git-appraise` (the most ambitious notes-based system) has had the same "Open" issues sitting for years — it works but never crossed the chasm ([git-appraise](https://github.com/google/git-appraise), [HN 2023](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=37084575)). Notes also require explicit `git fetch refs/notes/*:refs/notes/*` to share — a known UX cliff.

**Verdict:** notes are a viable *substrate* for tooling that pulls them programmatically, not a viable *UX surface* for humans browsing on github.com. Use them only if our UI never assumes the user can see them in a web view.

## 4. Check Runs vs commit statuses for non-App CLIs

This is unambiguous and load-bearing for `dr-gate`:

> **Write permission for the Check Runs REST API is only available to GitHub Apps.** OAuth apps and authenticated users can view check runs but cannot create them ([GitHub REST docs](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/checks/runs), [Ken Muse](https://www.kenmuse.com/blog/creating-github-checks/)).

The standard workaround when you don't want to ship a GitHub App: use the **commit status API** instead. Personal access tokens and `gh auth token` can write commit statuses freely. Cargo's release tooling and most CI integrations that don't ship as Apps default to statuses for exactly this reason. If `dr-gate` must show as a Check Run, it needs either (a) a real GitHub App with installation tokens, or (b) to run inside GitHub Actions where `GITHUB_TOKEN` has check-write scope by default ([authenticate-with-github_token](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/tutorials/authenticate-with-github_token)).

## 5. Auth-via-`gh` precedent

This pattern is real and well-precedented in Rust:

- The `gh-token` crate exists specifically to deserialize GitHub CLI's token from `~/.config/gh/hosts.yml` for Rust consumers ([lib.rs/gh-token](https://lib.rs/crates/gh-token)).
- `gh-config` provides the same functionality as a hybrid library/CLI ([crates.io/gh-config](https://crates.io/crates/gh-config)).
- `cargo-binstall` already attempts to retrieve tokens from `gh auth token` and git credential helpers as part of its auto-discovery ([cargo-binstall #1681](https://github.com/cargo-bins/cargo-binstall/issues/1681)).
- `release-plz` accepts `GITHUB_TOKEN` env var and is the standard recommendation for Rust release automation ([release-plz quickstart](https://release-plz.dev/docs/github/quickstart)).
- `gh auth token` is officially documented as a programmatic interface to extract the token ([gh docs](https://cli.github.com/manual/gh_auth_token)), and GitHub recommends it as a `git credential.helper` ([cli/cli #5081](https://github.com/cli/cli/discussions/5081)).

**Verdict: green light.** Inheriting from `gh auth token` is a normal Rust-CLI pattern with multiple production precedents.

## 6. Solo→team CLI evolution patterns

The empirical record:

- **Atuin** (200k+ devs) — went solo→team carefully, encrypted client-side, "exploring what happens when their open-source philosophy meets team workflows" ([Atuin home](https://atuin.sh/), [Changelog #579](https://changelog.com/podcast/579)). Team features added *after* solo product-market fit was clear.
- **Fig** — added Scripts/Dotfiles/Plugins/SSH-sharing as team features, got acquired by Amazon, **and all those team features were killed** in the migration to Amazon Q ([fig sunset](https://fig.io/blog/post/fig-is-sunsetting), [AWS docs](https://aws.amazon.com/blogs/devops/exploring-the-latest-features-of-the-amazon-q-developer-cli/)). The team stuff was the *first* thing to go.
- **Warp** — heavy team features tied to a $20/mo paywall; sustained Hacker News backlash about "paying for a terminal," with the most common comparison being "for $20 I could just buy Claude Code" ([HN 45772558](https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=45772558), [BigGo](https://finance.biggo.com/news/202510312004_Warp-Terminal-New-Pricing-Debate)).
- **Sapling (Meta)** — open-sourced client, but the server (Mononoke) stayed proprietary; near-zero adoption outside Meta ([Medium analysis](https://medium.com/@benneighbour/is-metas-sapling-the-future-of-vcs-3d106fcebce0)). Team features that depend on a server you can't run = dead on arrival.
- **lazygit** — stayed solo; no team-feature attempt; thriving.

**Pattern for success:** (1) nail solo first (Atuin), (2) team features are *opt-in and use existing substrates the user already has* (git remote, GitHub auth) rather than a new server, (3) avoid paywalling the team layer if the solo product was free (Warp's lesson). **Pattern for failure:** require a new server (Sapling/Mononoke), or bolt team features on as a monetization wedge (Warp, Fig pre-acquisition).

## 7. Verdict for each load-bearing pattern

| Pattern | Light | One-sentence reason |
|---|---|---|
| Auto-publish runs as draft PRs that update per turn | **Yellow** | Copilot coding agent and Cursor BugBot prove the UX works, but Sweep.dev abandoned this exact pattern and bot-PR fatigue is documented. |
| Commit `.deadreckon/runs/<id>/` artifact bundles | **Yellow→Red** | SpecStory's wrestling and Aider's deliberate gitignore both signal this is the friction-heavy choice; static config is fine, transcripts are not. |
| `dr-gate` as GitHub Check Runs | **Red** without a GitHub App | The Checks write API is App-only; CLI tools that aren't Apps must use commit statuses instead. |
| Git notes for team index | **Yellow** | Works as a tooling substrate (Gerrit, git-ai prove it), invisible on github.com web UI — only viable if our reader never assumes browser visibility. |
| Auth via `gh auth token` inheritance | **Green** | Standard pattern with multiple Rust crates (`gh-token`, `gh-config`) and tools (`cargo-binstall`) already doing it. |

## Five precedents we should explicitly mimic

1. **Copilot coding agent's "draft PR that updates per turn"** — the live-commits-as-turns metaphor is the proven UX ([GitHub Blog](https://github.blog/news-insights/product-news/github-copilot-meet-the-new-coding-agent/)).
2. **AGENTS.md as the in-repo agent contract** — 60k+ repos, now an LF standard; piggyback on it rather than inventing new files ([agents.md](https://agents.md/)).
3. **Renovate's grouping/`prHourlyLimit`** — the canonical answer to bot-PR fatigue; default to one PR per logical unit, not one per turn ([Renovate docs](https://docs.renovatebot.com/bot-comparison/)).
4. **`gh auth token` + `gh-token` crate** — proven Rust-CLI auth inheritance, no new credential surface ([lib.rs/gh-token](https://lib.rs/crates/gh-token)).
5. **Sourcegraph Amp's shareable thread URLs** — server-side thread store with a stable URL is winning over git-committed transcripts; consider this even if we still write to git ([Amp manual](https://ampcode.com/manual)).

## Three precedents we should explicitly avoid

1. **Sweep.dev's original "GitHub-issue-to-PR-bot" architecture** — the company that invented our exact pattern *pivoted away from it* to a JetBrains plugin ([sweep.dev](https://sweep.dev/)). That's the loudest signal in this report.
2. **GitHub Check Runs from a non-App CLI** — the API simply will not let you write checks without an App; building toward it is wasted engineering ([GitHub Checks REST docs](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/checks/runs)).
3. **Sapling/Mononoke's "team features need our server" trap** — any pattern that requires a deadreckon-hosted backend will replicate Sapling's near-zero external adoption ([Sapling analysis](https://medium.com/@benneighbour/is-metas-sapling-the-future-of-vcs-3d106fcebce0)).

## Context

deadreckon is a Rust agentic-CLI harness. We're considering team-sync via GitHub primitives:
- Auto-publish agentic runs as draft PRs that update per turn
- Commit `.deadreckon/runs/<id>/` artifact bundles into the squash commit
- Post `dr-gate` results as GitHub Check Runs (or commit statuses)
- Use git notes for a team index
- Authenticate via `gh auth token` inheritance

We need to know: **what tools have already tried this, and what happened?** Adoption signals — stars, downloads, sunset announcements, user complaints, replacements.

## Tools to investigate (use WebSearch + WebFetch)

### Direct precedents — agent runs published as PRs

- **GitHub Copilot Workspace** — is it still in technical preview? GA? sunset? What did adopters say? Look for retrospectives, post-mortems, user reviews from 2025–2026.
- **GitHub Copilot coding agent** (the more recent "assign-an-issue-to-Copilot" feature) — adoption, user reception. Is `@copilot` mention in PR comments actually used?
- **Devin (Cognition Labs)** — opens its own PRs. What's the adoption story? Pricing-model effect on adoption? User complaints about PR noise?
- **Sourcegraph Amp** — threads-as-shareable-URLs pattern. Adoption?
- **Cursor BugBot / background agents** — file PRs from agents. Adoption signals.
- **Aider** — does it integrate with GitHub PRs? (`aider --gui`, `aider /commit`). What do users actually use?
- **OpenAI Codex web** (the cloud one) — opens PRs. Adoption.
- **Jules (Google)** — same pattern.
- **Sweep (sweep.dev)** — was popular in 2024 for "GitHub issue to PR." Are they still around? What happened?
- **Sourcery / CodeRabbit / Greptile** — review-style not run-style, but their PR integration patterns are instructive.

For each: what's the user reception? Did it fade? Is there community pushback against "agent-opened PRs"? Search for "Renovate fatigue", "Dependabot fatigue", "agent PR noise" — the precedent for bot-PR backlash.

### Run-artifact-in-git precedents

- **SpecStory** — `.specstory/history/` checked into git. How widely adopted? Who uses it? Any complaints about repo bloat, secret leaks, merge conflicts?
- **Aider chat history** (`.aider.chat.history.md`) — committed to repos? Or gitignored?
- **Continue.dev `.continue/`** — committed?
- **`.cursor/rules/`** — committed; widespread.
- **`AGENTS.md`** — committed; widespread (60k+ repos per the standard).
- **OpenTelemetry GenAI traces** — anyone committing these to git? Or always shipped to an observability backend?

For run *transcripts* specifically (not static config), what's the adoption story for committing them to git? Is the field moving toward "transcripts in git" or "transcripts in cloud-only"?

### git notes — is anyone actually using it?

- Real-world git notes adoption in 2025–2026. The classic complaint is "GitHub doesn't render them." Has that changed?
- Tools that use git notes successfully: `git-imerge`? `gerrit`? others? What's the workflow that justifies the friction?
- Tools that tried and abandoned git notes — any documented?

### GitHub Check Runs by non-App tools

- Tools posting Check Runs as a CLI (not as a GitHub App) — possible? Any examples?
- Tools using commit statuses instead — adoption pattern?

### CLI auth via `gh auth token` inheritance

- Rust/Go/Node CLIs that use this pattern. Examples and reception.
- `cargo-dist` — does it use `gh` for releases?
- `dprint`, `cargo-binstall`, `cargo-mutants`, `release-plz` — auth patterns.

### Adjacent — "single-user CLI gone team"

Look at tools that started solo-CLI and tried to add team features. Did they succeed?
- **Fig / Amazon Q CLI** — tried to add team features; what happened?
- **Warp Terminal** — team features; adoption?
- **Atuin** (shell history sync) — solo to team; adoption signals.
- **lazygit** — stayed solo; why did they not add team features?
- **Sapling (Meta)** — what happened to it outside Meta?

What's the pattern for a solo CLI successfully adding team features vs failing?

## Commit Status API Scopes

For the GitHub commit status API, the repo:status OAuth scope grants targeted access to statuses without also granting access to repository code, while the repo scope grants permission to code as well as statuses.

When creating a personal access token for commit status operations, repo:status grants read/write access to public and private repository commit statuses.

For fine-grained personal access tokens specifically, Commit statuses: Read and write grants permission to create commit statuses.

## About "statuses:write"

It's worth noting that the search results do not specifically mention a "statuses:write" scope. The relevant scopes documented are:
- **Classic PATs**: `repo:status` (read/write access to commit statuses)
- **Fine-grained PATs**: "Commit Statuses" permission with "Read and write" access level

If you're looking for the latest GitHub documentation on fine-grained token scopes, you may want to check the [GitHub official docs](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/commits/statuses) directly, as scope naming conventions may have evolved.

Based on the search results, here's what I found regarding GitHub API rate limits and secondary content creation limits:

## Primary Rate Limit

For GitHub Apps, the base limit for non-GitHub Enterprise Cloud Organizations is 5,000 requests per hour.

## Secondary Rate Limits for Content Creation

In general, no more than 80 content-generating requests per minute and no more than 500 content-generating requests per hour are allowed. This is lower than the primary 5,000 request limit and specifically applies to content creation activities.

Rapid content creation on GitHub is listed as one of the triggers for secondary rate limits. Content creation limits include actions taken on the GitHub web interface as well as via the REST API and GraphQL API.

## Response to Exceeding Limits

If you exceed a secondary rate limit, you will receive a 403 or 429 response and an error message that indicates that you exceeded a secondary rate limit. If the retry-after response header is present, you should not retry your request until after that many seconds has elapsed.

The search results don't show a specific 5000 secondary content creation per hour limit mentioned in any 2025 documentation. The generally documented limit for content creation is 500 requests per hour as mentioned above.

## Octocrab ETag Support

Octocrab takes an optional etag which allows for efficient polling. The library provides built-in support for ETag-based conditional requests through its `Etagged` type.

Here's how it works in octocrab:

You can make a request returning an `Etagged<Page<Event>>` response, and if the page value is present, process it; otherwise the data hasn't changed. The etag from the response can be stored and used in the next iteration.

## API Pattern

The search results show that octocrab implements ETag support through an `.etag()` method on request builders. For example, the organization events API demonstrates this pattern where you can pass the previously stored ETag to subsequent requests for efficient polling of data that hasn't changed.

# How `gh` Handles Multiple Accounts

## Account Management

Since v2.40.0, `gh` supports multiple accounts per host. The `auth login` command is now additive rather than replacing existing tokens. Users can switch between accounts using `gh auth switch`, which "swap[s] the token used by `gh` for API requests, and for git operations when `gh` was configured as a git credential manager."

## Token Selection with `gh auth token`

The `gh auth token` command works with the currently active account by default. However, you can specify a particular account using the `--user` flag in combination with `--hostname` for non-interactive scenarios. For example:

```
GH_TOKEN=$(gh auth token --user williammartin) gh api /user
```

This allows you to explicitly retrieve a token for a specific user rather than relying on the active account.

## Behavior in CI Environments

The documentation doesn't explicitly address CI behavior, but the `--user` flag exists specifically to "disambiguate accounts when running non-interactively"—suggesting CI use cases are supported. By setting the `GH_TOKEN` environment variable with a specific user's token, you can control which account is used in automated workflows.
```

Based on the web search results, here's what I found about Dependabot and Renovate fatigue and bot PR noise complaints:

## Key Findings on Bot Fatigue and PR Noise

### The Problem: "Alert Fatigue"

If you have a monorepo or a project with many dependencies, logging in on Monday morning to find 50 separate PRs is overwhelming, leading to "alert fatigue," where developers simply close PRs without looking or ignore them entirely.

A dependency management tool that creates dozens of PRs per week can overwhelm your team and lead to update fatigue.

### Dependabot's Noise Issues

For repositories with many dependencies, Renovate's rate limiting prevents the flood of PRs that Dependabot can create when first enabled. More specifically, Dependabot tends to be noisier because it creates separate PRs for each dependency. For a project with 50 dependencies, you might see 10-15 PRs per week during active periods.

Dependabot creates one PR per dependency, so for 100 projects, you get 100 PRs.

### Renovate's Solution: Grouping

Renovate's biggest advantage over Dependabot is its ability to group updates. Instead of 20 PRs for 20 different eslint plugins, Renovate can intelligently bundle them into a single PR titled "Update ESLint packages." This single feature reduces noise by 80-90% in complex projects.

Additionally, Renovate even supports branch automerge (merging without creating a PR at all) for low-risk updates, which further reduces noise.

### Recognition in Industry

After optimizing dependency workflows for hundreds of clients, strategies have been developed for managing Dependabot at scale without sacrificing velocity.

Based on the search results, here's information about `gh auth token`, the `GITHUB_TOKEN` environment variable, and their precedence in Codespaces:

## Environment Variable Precedence

GH_TOKEN and GITHUB_TOKEN are authentication tokens checked in order of precedence, with GH_TOKEN taking priority. Setting these environment variables avoids being prompted to authenticate and takes precedence over previously stored credentials.

## Codespaces Context

By default, a codespace has a very-restricted GITHUB_TOKEN that has access only to the repo for which the codespace was created. Codespaces uses GITHUB_TOKEN, but the token it puts there is very restrictive because they want to be careful about what they give the Codespace permission to do.

## Known Issues

There have been reports of unexpected behavior in Codespaces. Even though GH_TOKEN should have higher precedence than GITHUB_TOKEN, it seems gh somehow uses the latter within Codespaces. When using Codespaces, the value of the GITHUB_TOKEN environment variable is being used for authentication, and to have GitHub CLI store credentials instead, first clear the value from the environment.

## CI/GitHub Actions Usage

To use gh in GitHub Actions, add GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }} to env.

## SpecStory Overview

SpecStory is the intent layer for modern software development that automatically saves AI conversations across tools as clean markdown. It automatically saves all AI coding interactions in .specstory/history, and the history lives in your repo alongside code in a git-friendly markdown format.

## Git Adoption Challenges and Complaints

There are notable concerns about using SpecStory with Git in team environments:

**Repository Bloat Concerns:** Some users have put .specstory in .gitignore because everyone's files would be mixed in together.

**Team Collaboration Issues:** Some developers collaborate with 1-2 others on projects on GitHub where they check in their specstory history, but a current pain point when using it with Cursor chat is there is always some late specstory that needs to get added to the commit history (oftentimes after the branch has already been merged).

**Acknowledged by Developers:** The SpecStory team is actively thinking about ways to make SpecStory more friendly to team environments, and have plans around this.

The core tension is between wanting to preserve intent and decision-making history in Git while avoiding repository bloat and team coordination issues when multiple developers are working on the same project.

## Chat History File

The default chat history file for Aider is `.aider.chat.history.md`. This file is stored at the repo root by default, and the chat history is human-readable Markdown, easy to grep.

## Gitignore Configuration

Aider creates a .gitignore with `.aider*` to prevent users from accidentally adding aider files to git. This pattern would match `.aider.chat.history.md` and other aider-related files, preventing them from being committed to version control.

This makes sense as a best practice - the chat history file contains conversation logs between you and the AI, which are typically local to your development session and shouldn't be shared across team members or stored in version control history.

If you want to share specific chat history logs, you can copy the markdown logs you want to share from .aider.chat.history.md and make a github gist, or publish the raw markdown logs on the web any way you'd like.

```text
# Git Notes Merge: Concurrent Writes and Strategies

## How Git Notes Merge Works for Concurrent Writes

When multiple people write notes to the same commit, `git notes merge` attempts to reconcile conflicting changes. The process:

1. **Detects conflicts** between the local notes ref and a remote notes ref being merged
2. **Applies a merge strategy** to resolve conflicts automatically (or manually)
3. **Creates a merge worktree** at `.git/NOTES_MERGE_WORKTREE` for manual resolution
4. **Finalizes or aborts** the merge with `--commit` or `--abort`

From the documentation:

> If conflicts arise and a strategy for automatically resolving conflicting notes is not given, the `manual` resolver is used. This resolver checks out the conflicting notes in a special worktree (`.git/NOTES_MERGE_WORKTREE`), and instructs the user to manually resolve the conflicts there.

## The Five Merge Strategies

### 1. **manual** (default)
- Checks out conflicting notes in `.git/NOTES_MERGE_WORKTREE`
- Requires user to manually resolve conflicts
- User then runs `git notes merge --commit` or `git notes merge --abort`

### 2. **ours**
> Automatically resolves conflicting notes in favor of the local version (i.e. the current notes ref).

### 3. **theirs**
> Automatically resolves notes conflicts in favor of the remote version (i.e. the given notes ref being merged into the current notes ref).

### 4. **union**
> Automatically resolves notes conflicts by concatenating the local and remote versions.

### 5. **cat_sort_uniq**
> Similar to `union`, but in addition to concatenating the local and remote versions, this strategy also sorts the resulting lines, and removes duplicate lines from the result. This is equivalent to applying the "cat | sort | uniq" shell pipeline to the local and remote versions.

**Best for**: Line-based note formats where duplicates should be avoided.

## Auto-Resolution for Concurrent Writes

**Yes, concurrent writes can be auto-resolved**, but only with explicit strategy selection. Use:

```bash
git notes merge -s <strategy> <notes-ref>
```

Or configure the default strategy:

```bash
git config notes.mergeStrategy union  # or ours, theirs, cat_sort_uniq
```

**Without specifying a strategy, the `manual` strategy is used by default**, requiring human intervention.
```
</details></tool-use>

## Key Findings

**Cargo Credential Process & Keyring Support:**
Cargo supports fetching tokens from secrets storage systems, such as a password manager or the system keyring through the credential-process feature. The more advanced "Cargo" kind of credential process supports different actions passed as a command-line argument, intended for more pleasant integration experience, at the expense of requiring a Cargo-specific process to glue to the password manager.

**Keyring Pattern for MacOS:**
On macOS, you can store your credentials for each host in the System Keychain, and then have Cargo read it from there by telling Git to store credentials in the system keychain.

**Git Credential Helper Integration:**
HTTPS authentication requires the credential.helper mechanism, with multiple credential helpers that you specify in your global git configuration file.

**Cargo-binstall GitHub Token Issue:**
The search results include a report of an issue where a GitHub token works for pulling Cargo.toml from a GitHub repo, but then fails for some other requests for the same URL.

The general pattern for secure token storage with Cargo tools involves using system keyring capabilities through git credential helpers or Cargo's credential-process configuration, which keeps tokens out of plaintext configuration files.

Based on the search results, I found information about the requirements for using `gh pr create --draft` with empty branches or zero commits:

## Key Findings

Users attempting to create a PR without immediately adding changes encounter the error "No commits between main and hotfix/testing". A feature request has been made to provide a flag such as `--allow-empty` to let users create a PR with no changes.

Draft PRs (`--draft`) allow pushing work-in-progress changes for early feedback without formal review requests, however, the `--draft` flag does not bypass the requirement for commits between branches.

## The Issue

Currently, the `gh pr create` command fails with GraphQL errors including "No commits between" when attempting to create a pull request from an empty branch or a branch with zero commits relative to the base. This happens even when using the `--draft` flag, as draft status doesn't exempt a PR from requiring at least some commit difference between the branches.

The limitation appears to be a GitHub platform requirement rather than a CLI-specific restriction, as it's been labeled as a platform problem rather than a CLI client problem.

## Base URL Configuration

Octocrab allows you to set the base URL for the client. You can configure this using the OctocrabBuilder with a method like `.base_uri("https://github.example.com")?` for self-hosted or GitHub Enterprise instances.

## Example Usage

The OctocrabBuilder is a builder struct for Octocrab that allows you to configure the client, such as using GitHub previews, the GitHub instance, authentication, etc.

The documentation shows this practical example for configuring a custom base URL:

```rust
let octocrab = octocrab::OctocrabBuilder::default()
    .add_preview("machine-man")
    .base_uri("https://github.example.com")?
    .build()?
```

This approach enables Octocrab to work with GitHub Enterprise Server or any self-hosted GitHub instance by simply changing the base URL to point to your custom domain instead of the default GitHub.com API endpoint.

## Git Notes Adoption and Display

GitHub opted to stop displaying commit notes in 2014 without much explanation, which has historically limited adoption of the feature. However, there are signs of renewed interest:

**Recent Tools Using Git Notes:**

Git AI built the open standard for tracking AI-generated code with Git Notes, representing a modern use case for the feature. A Git Note with AI-attributions is attached to the commit through their post-commit workflow.

**Git Notes Capabilities:**

Git notes let you attach metadata to commits or other Git objects without altering their history, functioning as sticky notes for your repository—perfect for adding context like bug references or CI statuses while keeping the commit history untouched.

**Display Challenges:**

It doesn't make much sense to display non-text-format notes with git log, so if you use such notes, you'll probably need to write some special-purpose tools to do something useful with them.

The search results indicate that while git notes have historically suffered from limited adoption and poor platform support, there are emerging 2025 tools—particularly in the AI coding space—that are leveraging git notes for metadata tracking and attribution purposes.

Based on the search results, here's what I found about GitHub Check Runs API authentication with CLI vs non-app methods:

## Key Differences

**Check Runs API Restrictions:**
Write permission for the REST API to interact with checks is only available to GitHub Apps. To create a check run, you must use a GitHub App. OAuth apps and authenticated users can view check runs and check suites, but they are not able to create them.

**GitHub App Authentication with CLI:**
Using the gh CLI is the easiest way to interact with the API and it's easiest to auth with an APP as a non-user and control access to it via app installation. You just need to create an installation token and utilize that when interacting with the gh CLI.

The actions/create-github-app-token action can generate an installation access token, which the workflow then uses to make an API request via the GitHub CLI.

**Non-App Authentication Limitations:**
If you're not building a GitHub App, you might be interested in using the REST API to interact with commit statuses as an alternative, since non-app authentication cannot create check runs.

**General Recommendation:**
If you want to use the API for an organization or on behalf of another user, GitHub recommends that you use a GitHub App.

In summary: The Check Runs API exclusively requires GitHub App authentication for write operations via CLI or any other method, while non-app authentication (personal access tokens, OAuth apps) can only view check runs.

## BugBot Overview

BugBot finds bugs directly in GitHub, automatically reviews PRs, comments on potential issues, and provides fixes directly in your Cursor editor or through Background Agent. When enabled, Bugbot automatically runs in the background on new PRs.

## Background Agents

Background agents, currently in beta, allows developers to create agents which run in a remote environment provisioned by Cursor. The agent will clone a GitHub repository, work on a separate branch, and push changes. Bugbot Autofix is an early example of agents running automatically based on an event like PR creation.

## Adoption and PR Creation

Over 35% of Bugbot Autofix changes are merged into the base PR. Autofix is now out of beta and available to all Bugbot users. Since Background Agent was released in early access a few weeks ago, early signals have been positive. The company expanded Background Agent to all users.

## Performance Metrics

The average number of issues identified per run has nearly doubled in the last six months, while the resolution rate (percentage of bugs resolved by users before the PR is merged) has increased from 52% to 76%. 70%+ of flags get resolved before merge.
